title: Death of Stars: White Dwarfs and Supernovae

cards.h: We are made of dead stars
cards.b: The hydrogen and most helium in the universe came from the Big Bang. Nearly everything else, the carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe, the calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, was made inside stars and scattered when they died. Stellar death is also the source of black holes and neutron stars.

Stars below about 8 Suns end quietly as white dwarfs; those above about 8 Suns end in a supernova. The less massive the star, the slower and gentler the death. Red dwarfs will take trillions of years; none has yet died.

When hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats and hydrogen burns in a shell around it. The outer layers swell and cool: a red giant. In about 5 billion years the Sun will reach near Earth's present orbit. The star later puffs off its outer layers as a glowing shell, called a planetary nebula (a misleading name from early telescopes; they have nothing to do with planets).

cards.h: White dwarf: a cooling Earth-sized star
cards.b: What remains is the hot core: a white dwarf, the mass of the Sun in a body the size of Earth. A teaspoon would weigh several tonnes. It no longer fuses; it only cools slowly. It is held up not by heat but by electron degeneracy pressure, a quantum effect of crowded electrons.

In 1930, aged 19, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculated that this quantum pressure can only hold up a white dwarf of up to about 1.4 Suns. Heavier, and gravity wins. This Chandrasekhar limit was fiercely disputed by Eddington, but proved right, and earned Chandrasekhar the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Type Ia: a white dwarf in a binary pulls gas from its partner, or merges with another, until it nears 1.4 Suns and detonates as a thermonuclear explosion. All explode with nearly the same brightness, so they serve as standard candles for cosmic distances.

Core-collapse (Type II): a massive star's iron core can no longer be supported; in under a second it collapses to a neutron star or black hole while the outer layers bounce off and explode, briefly outshining a whole galaxy.

Supernovae forge and spread elements heavier than iron too. Gold and platinum come largely from neutron star collisions (confirmed in 2017). The ejected material seeds new nebulae, which form new stars and planets enriched with heavy elements: our Solar System is a third-generation product.

Chinese astronomers recorded the 1054 CE 'guest star' that left the Crab Nebula. Tycho (1572) and Kepler (1604) saw supernovae in our galaxy; none since. SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud was seen in February 1987, and neutrinos from its core were detected on Earth hours before the light, confirming core collapse.

• 'The Sun will go supernova.' It is too light.
  • 'A supernova is a new star.' It is the death of one. The Latin name nova means new, from old naming.
  • 'White dwarfs are tiny in mass.' They hold roughly a Sun's mass.

Chandrasekhar was born in Lahore (1910), nephew of C.V. Raman, and studied at Presidency College, Madras. On the ship to England in 1930 he worked out the mass limit of white dwarfs. He spent his career at the University of Chicago; NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory (1999) is named for him. In India, AstroSat studies supernova remnants in X-rays.

• Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs; stars over about 8 Suns explode.
  • The Chandrasekhar limit, 1.4 Suns, caps a white dwarf's mass.
  • Type Ia supernovae are standard candles; Type II create neutron stars or black holes.
  • Supernovae spread heavy elements that build planets and life.

Think about it: (1) Why are Type Ia explosions so similar? (2) What does 'we are star dust' mean in physics terms?
